one_line: Better Stack tours the late-2025 Codex CLI update (Rust rewrite, ChatGPT login, sandbox and approval modes, config profiles) and candidly compares it with Claude Code.
summary: The host says they avoided Codex CLI because it felt buggy and GPT coding models trailed Claude, but a recent update changed that. OpenAI's terminal agent was rewritten from TypeScript (Ink) to Rust (Ratatui), which the host finds faster, and it now offers a minimal text-only UI and sign-in with a ChatGPT plan. The video covers transcript inspection, the default sandbox and its three modes, approval policies that are configured separately from the sandbox, and config.toml with named profiles, reasoning settings, a notify script and OpenAI-compatible model endpoints (only GPT-OSS worked for the host). A feature comparison concludes that Claude Code is well ahead on features and documentation, though Codex is a reasonable base to build on. The video closes with OpenAI's open-source fund offering up to $25,000 in API credits and a note that Windows is not officially supported. Overall this is a practical overview with some config detail, not a deep benchmark or internals study.

key_ideas.idea: Codex CLI was rewritten from TypeScript (Ink) to Rust (Ratatui) for speed, fewer dependencies and better security; the host finds the Rust build faster
key_ideas.detail: Minimal text-only UI with no ASCII art. Sign-in with a ChatGPT plan or API key is offered at first run. The host's experience of speed is anecdotal.

key_ideas.idea: The agent's reasoning and tool calls are inspectable through a transcript view
key_ideas.detail: Pressing Esc twice or Ctrl+T opens a view showing bash commands run, files read and the model's thinking. Q returns to the main layout.

key_ideas.idea: Sandbox is on by default and confines execution to the project workspace (files, processes, network)
key_ideas.detail: A sandbox flag offers three modes: Workspace Write (edit files in the directory without approval), Read Only (reads without approval, asks before edits or commands) and a full-access mode the host calls 'dangerous access'.

key_ideas.idea: Approval policy is a separate axis from the sandbox, which the host finds confusing
key_ideas.detail: Four approval policies are named: on-request, never, on-failure (ask only to retry a failed command) and untrusted (run only trusted commands). Combining them with sandbox modes sets the autonomy level.

key_ideas.idea: config.toml can hold sandbox and approval values plus named profiles selected with -p, along with reasoning effort, summary, verbosity and a notify script
key_ideas.detail: The host compares the notify script to Claude Code hooks, but notes Codex's notify docs are a small section.

key_ideas.idea: Non-OpenAI models work only if they expose an OpenAI-compatible API and support the tool calls Codex expects
key_ideas.detail: The host got GPT-OSS working. DeepSeek failed, which the host suspects is either a config issue or missing tool support.

key_ideas.idea: On features, Claude Code is ahead by the host's account, and Codex is not yet a replacement
key_ideas.detail: Items listed for Claude Code: custom prompts with arguments, custom status line, hooks, custom sub-agents, output styles, visual context, session resume, background tasks, vim mode, security review, and more detailed docs.

key_ideas.idea: OpenAI's open-source fund gives up to $25,000 in API credits to open-source projects that use Codex CLI and OpenAI models
key_ideas.detail: Presented as a practical incentive to adopt Codex CLI; the host does not verify eligibility details.

techniques.name: Separate sandbox from approval when setting agent autonomy
techniques.how: Pick a sandbox mode (Workspace Write, Read Only or full access) and an approval policy (on-request, never, on-failure, untrusted) independently; check the active values with /status. The host did not show exact flag spellings.
techniques.when: Choosing how much an agent may do unattended, e.g. read-only review versus a trusted YOLO-style run.

techniques.name: Named config profiles in config.toml run with -p
techniques.how: Put sandbox and approval values, model and reasoning settings in config.toml, define them as a named profile and launch with the -p flag. The host did not show the TOML syntax.
techniques.when: Switching quickly between a restricted review mode and a permissive run mode.

techniques.name: Audit an agent run via the transcript view
techniques.how: Press Ctrl+T (or Esc twice) during a session to see every bash command, file read and reasoning step; press Q to go back.
techniques.when: Checking what an agent actually executed before trusting its result.

techniques.name: Tune model and reasoning effort per task
techniques.how: Use /model to see and select the model (GPT-5 is the default, no nano or mini), then set reasoning effort in the config. The host says GPT-5 at high reasoning is good for coding.
techniques.when: Harder coding tasks where a higher reasoning level is worth the cost.

techniques.name: Point Codex at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for non-OpenAI models
techniques.how: Configure a custom OpenAI-compatible provider in config.toml. GPT-OSS worked for the host; DeepSeek returned an error. The provider keys were not shown.
techniques.when: Trying open-weight models behind an OpenAI-style API, provided they support tool calls.

techniques.name: Notify script for event alerts
techniques.how: Set a notification script in config.toml, which the host compares to Claude Code hooks. Details were not shown.
techniques.when: Getting alerted when a long agent turn finishes.

techniques.name: Everyday workflow commands
techniques.how: /init creates AGENTS.md (not a tool-specific file); /status shows workspace, model, token usage and sandbox/approval settings; /model shows the model. Use @ to attach files, Ctrl+V to paste images, and non-interactive mode for scripted runs. Custom prompts live in a prompts folder and run as commands.
techniques.when: Starting a repo's agent instructions, attaching context, scripting Codex runs, and reusing prompts.

numbers.claim: Codex CLI has 11 default slash commands
Four approval policies: on-request, never, on-failure, untrusted
OpenAI open-source fund gives up to $25,000 in API credits for projects using Codex CLI and OpenAI models
Default model is GPT-5 (no nano or mini shown)

hot_takes: Claude Code is 'way ahead' of Codex CLI on features and documentation, so Codex is not yet a replacement, though it is a good base to build on.
Rust rewrite is faster in the host's experience.
Creating AGENTS.md instead of a tool-specific markdown file is a welcome convention.
Security-first sandbox default is a strength, but sandbox and approval combinations are confusing.
The $25k open-source credits fund is presented as a reason to try Codex.

relevance.why: Codex's sandbox modes and approval policies are a reference point for Crucible's opt-in sandboxed execution and exec-gate guardrails.
relevance.action: Compare Codex's three sandbox modes and four approval policies with Crucible's exec-gate design and note where a per-run profile would fit.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code CLI and handles approvals. Codex's separation of sandbox and approval policy, and its named profiles, are relevant prior art.
relevance.action: Look at how Codex's on-request, on-failure and untrusted policies and -p profiles map onto ProsHarness approval handling.
